content: The use of atovaquone/proguanil for prophylaxis is not recommended in patients with a creatinine clearance (CrCl) of less than 30 mL/min. In such cases, it should only be used for treatment if the benefits significantly outweigh the risks. For patients with a CrCl between 30 and 80 mL/min, no dosage adjustments are necessary. The medication should be taken at the same time each day with food or a milky drink. For children who have difficulty swallowing, the tablets may be crushed and mixed with condensed milk immediately before administration. Atovaquone and proguanil have potential drug interactions. Topical dapsone should not be co-administered with oral dapsone or antimalarial medications due to the risk of hemolytic reactions. Efavirenz decreases the levels of atovaquone and proguanil through an unspecified mechanism, and alternative drugs should be considered. Indinavir reduces atovaquone levels by an unknown mechanism, requiring close monitoring or therapy modification. Metoclopramide, particularly in its intranasal form, may increase atovaquone levels, but it can also reduce its absorption when taken orally. Similarly, tetracycline may decrease atovaquone levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption, though the clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. Rifabutin and rifampin reduce atovaquone levels by increasing its metabolism, necessitating caution and close monitoring. Atovaquone may enhance the effects of warfarin, requiring careful monitoring. Common side effects of atovaquone/proguanil include abdominal pain (3–31%), elevated transaminases (17–27%), headache (3–14%), vomiting (1–13%), nausea (12%), asthenia (8%), diarrhea (1–8%), pruritus (6%), anorexia (5%), dizziness (5%), dyspepsia (1–4%), and gastritis (0–3%). Rare adverse effects include neutropenia, anemia, pancytopenia (in patients with severe renal impairment treated with proguanil), allergic reactions (e.g., angioedema, urticaria, anaphylaxis, vasculitis), seizures, psychotic events (e.g., hallucinations), stomatitis, elevated liver function tests, hepatitis, cholestasis, photosensitivity, rash, erythema multiforme, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Prophylactic use in patients with severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30 mL/min) does not provide a radical cure or prevent delayed primary attacks of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale. Patients with severe malaria are not candidates for oral therapy, and the drug has not been evaluated for cerebral malaria or severe manifestations such as hyperparasitemia, pulmonary edema, or renal failure. Hepatitis and elevated transaminase levels have been reported with prophylactic use, requiring close monitoring, especially in patients with pre-existing hepatic impairment. Liver enzyme elevations may persist for up to four weeks after treatment ends. Absorption of atovaquone may be reduced in patients with diarrhea or vomiting, necessitating close monitoring and consideration of antiemetic use. Severe cases may require alternative antimalarial therapy. Monotherapy with atovaquone/proguanil may lead to parasite relapse in P. vivax malaria. Recurrent P. falciparum infections or chemoprophylactic failure after monotherapy should be treated with a different schizonticide. Prophylaxis should not be discontinued prematurely, as delayed cases of P. falciparum malaria may occur. Complete prophylaxis includes medication, protective clothing, insect repellents, and bed nets. No chemoprophylactic regimen is 100% effective, and patients should seek medical care for any febrile illness. Treatment failure has been reported in patients weighing over 100 kg, necessitating monitoring and follow-up in this group. Pregnant women are at higher risk of death and serious complications from P. falciparum malaria. Atovaquone/proguanil is classified as pregnancy category C. Proguanil is excreted in small amounts in breast milk, but the excretion of atovaquone is unknown, so caution is advised during lactation. Atovaquone is primarily excreted unchanged in feces (94%), while proguanil is excreted in urine (40–60%).
